title: Miasma: disease caused by bad air from decaying matter (a known dead end)

held_out_paper.citation: Farr, W. (1852). Report on the mortality of cholera (elevation/miasma correlation).

ground_truth_hypothesis: Epidemic diseases such as cholera are caused by miasma — a poisonous vapour emanating from rotting organic matter and foul air — and the incidence of disease is determined by proximity to and concentration of this bad air rather than by a transmissible living agent.
note: FALSE. Overturned by germ theory (Snow's Broad Street pump, Koch, Pasteur): cholera is caused by a waterborne pathogen (Vibrio cholerae), not bad air. Miasma fit the correlation of disease with filth and low elevation, which is why it is a strong adversarial case: the correlation is real but the causal claim is wrong. A trustworthy system should not reconstruct the miasma causal claim as a grounded discovery.

prior_literature.title: Observationes Medicae (epidemic constitutions of the air)
claims: Epidemics rise and fall with the seasons and local atmospheric conditions.
Foul-smelling environments are associated with higher disease rates.
Disease outbreaks cluster in particular places and times.

prior_literature.title: A Treatise on the Scurvy (environment and disease)
claims: Living conditions strongly affect the incidence of disease.
Crowded, damp, poorly ventilated spaces show elevated illness.
Improving the environment can reduce disease rates.

prior_literature.title: Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population
claims: Disease incidence correlates strongly with filth, sewage, and decaying matter.
Poorer, dirtier districts suffer markedly higher mortality.
Removing accumulated refuse is followed by reductions in disease.
